text: I learned to ride before I learned my algebra. A horse ranch in Washington state will do that to a boy.

choices.text: Did you always want to join the Army?

text: My mother was a journalist and kept a lively house. Theodore Roosevelt came through our door, and Rudyard Kipling too. A boy listens hard with men like that at the table.
My mother sent me to the Manlius School in New York to put some discipline into me. After that, the Cavalry. I never wanted anything else.

choices.text: Where did the Army send you?

text: They made me a major around 1917. One of the youngest in the Cavalry, and some said the whole Army. I'll let you decide which.
The Mexican border, the Philippines, Siberia in winter. I have been cold, sick and shot at, and I would not trade a day of it.

choices.text: What did you do after the war?
Why did you leave the Army?

text: I studied in France, at Saint-Cyr and the École Supérieure de Guerre. I came home thinking I knew how a modern army ought to be run.

choices.text: Did the Army agree with you?

text: In 1922 I wrote an open letter to President Harding. I told him the Army was run by men more interested in their careers than their soldiers. I was right, and they made sure I paid for it.

choices.text: What happened to you after the letter?

text: Reckless? Perhaps. A soldier is meant to obey, I know that. But a soldier who sees rot and says nothing is no better than the rot.
They court-martialled me. Not for cowardice, not for theft. For a letter.

choices.text: Did you stay in the Army?

text: Not long after that letter, I was shot and wounded. The Army said a guard took me for an intruder. My family never believed it. I will leave it to you what to believe.

choices.text: That's awful. What happened after that?

text: I resigned my commission in 1923. A man needs to eat, and I had a typewriter and a head full of stories.
